lessons.title: Revelation, Visions and Miracles
lessons.description: Christian belief in revelation through the Bible and Jesus, visions, miracles and Humanist counter-arguments.
lessons.content_html:
Revelation: How God Makes Himself Known

Revelation is the means by which God communicates himself and his purposes to human beings. Christians believe that God has revealed himself progressively throughout history. A key framework for understanding this is the idea of covenants — formal agreements God established with key figures that progressively disclosed his character and plan. The covenant with Noah (Genesis 6–9) promised that God would never again destroy all life by flood, revealing his faithfulness and mercy. The covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15, 17) promised him descendants as numerous as the stars and a land for his people, revealing God as a personal God who initiates relationships.

The New Testament presents Jesus as the culmination of all revelation. Hebrews 1:1–4 states: “In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son.” For Christians across denominations, Jesus is not just a messenger but the living Word of God — the fullest possible expression of who God is and what he is like.

Key Fact

The covenant with Noah reveals God’s faithfulness and care for all creation. The covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15) reveals God as a personal God who initiates a relationship with a chosen people. Both are examples of God’s gradual self-disclosure that culminates in Jesus (Hebrews 1:1–4).

Visions as Evidence for God

Throughout the Bible, God communicates through visions. Genesis 15 records God appearing to Abraham in a vision, showing him the stars and promising him descendants — this covenant vision is foundational to the entire biblical story. Matthew 17:1–13 records the Transfiguration: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a mountain where his appearance is transformed — his face shines like the sun and his clothes become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear with him, and God’s voice declares from a cloud: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased. Listen to him.”

Christians understand the Transfiguration as a vision that revealed Jesus’s divine nature to his disciples. It confirmed their belief that he was not merely a prophet (like Moses or Elijah) but the Son of God himself. Christians today may have their own experiences of visions — reported encounters with God, angels or deceased saints — though different denominations respond to these with varying degrees of openness: Catholics have a formal process of approval for reported visions; many Protestants emphasise that scripture is the primary source of revelation.

Catholic Christianity has a tradition of formally recognised visions — Lourdes, Fatima, and the visions of Joan of Arc are evaluated by Church authority and may be approved. Catholics believe the Church’s Magisterium can discern genuine visions from false ones. Most Protestant and evangelical Christians emphasise that the Bible alone (sola scriptura) contains the authoritative revelation, and personal visions should always be tested against scripture. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians actively expect ongoing prophetic visions and experiences, believing the Spirit continues to reveal God directly to believers today. What unites all these views is agreement that God is capable of communicating with human beings — the debate is about the channels and the authority they carry.

Miracles as Evidence for God

A miracle is an event that goes beyond what science can explain, which believers attribute to God. Christians point to the miracles of Jesus as evidence both that God exists and that Jesus is who he claimed to be. John 4:43–54 records one such sign: a royal official whose son was near death asked Jesus for help. Jesus told him to go home, that his son would live. The official trusted Jesus’s word, and when he returned home, his servants told him his son had recovered at the exact moment Jesus had spoken. This sign strengthened the faith of the official’s whole household.

Atheists and Humanists challenge the evidential value of both visions and miracles. Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) argued that the uniform experience of natural law makes it always more rational to doubt a miracle report than to accept it — it is always more likely that the witnesses were mistaken, deceived or self-deceived than that an actual law of nature was suspended. Modern atheists such as Richard Dawkins argue that religious visions are hallucinations produced by brain chemistry, not genuine encounters with God. Humanists add that belief in miracles encourages people to reject medicine and science in favour of prayer and superstition. Christians respond that these objections assume the answer before looking at the evidence, and that the documented cases of miraculous healing and the transformed lives of vision-recipients cannot simply be dismissed.

Key Fact

David Hume argued in the eighteenth century that natural law is so reliable that it is always more rational to doubt a miracle report than to accept it. Christians respond that this assumes the conclusion before examining evidence, and that Hume’s argument would equally dismiss well-attested historical events that are surprising but real.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark “Explain Two with Sources,” cite either Hebrews 1:1–4 (revelation through Jesus) or Genesis 15 (Abraham covenant vision) or John 4:43–54 (the royal official’s son). A paraphrase without the reference earns only 4 marks at most. For the 12-mark Discuss question, remember to develop the Hume/Dawkins counter-argument in full — examiners note that students often write only one sentence on the opposing view. For divergent Christian views on visions, contrast Catholic (formal approval process, Magisterium) with Protestant (scripture as the primary test). SPaG marks reward correct spelling of: covenant, revelation, Transfiguration, Hume.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians believe God has revealed himself through covenants (Noah, Abraham) and most fully through Jesus — Hebrews 1:1–4 establishes Jesus as God’s definitive Word.
  • The Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–13) and the covenant vision to Abraham (Genesis 15) are key biblical visions used as evidence for God’s existence and character. Different denominations differ on how to evaluate claimed visions today.
  • Miracles, such as the healing of the royal official’s son (John 4:43–54), are used as evidence of divine action; Hume and Dawkins challenge this, but Christians argue these objections beg the question.

practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a mountain (1); his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light; Moses and Elijah appeared with him (1); God's voice declared from a cloud 'This is my Son whom I love — listen to him' (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe the covenants with Noah and Abraham provide evidence for God's existence.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe miracles provide evidence for the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The healing in John 4:43-54 — where the official's son recovered at the exact moment Jesus spoke — suggests God has power over natural processes, supporting belief in an omnipotent creator (2); miracles produce faith in those who witness them, suggesting they originate from a divine source rather than natural coincidence (2); source credit for citing John 4:43-54 or Hebrews 1:1-4 explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Miracles and visions prove that God exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: miracles (John 4:43-54) and visions (Genesis 15, Matthew 17:1-13) show God communicating directly; transformed lives and unexplained healings support this. Counter: Hume's argument that natural law always makes doubt more rational than acceptance; Dawkins on visions as brain chemistry; only anecdote supports miracles. Evaluate which position is stronger with reasoning. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: revelation, covenant, Transfiguration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views about visions, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Catholic Christianity formally evaluates reported visions through the Church's Magisterium — only approved visions are accepted as reliable, with Hebrews 1:1-4 confirming that any vision must align with Christ as the fullness of revelation (2); many Protestant Christians hold that scripture (sola scriptura) is the sole reliable source of revelation, so personal visions should always be tested against biblical teaching — the Transfiguration (Matthew 17) is paradigmatic but personal visions today are secondary to scripture (2); source credit for Hebrews 1:1-4 or Matthew 17:1-13 explicitly named (1).

lessons.title: Religious Experience, Prayer, Design and Cosmological Arguments
lessons.description: Religious experience, answered prayer, the design argument and Aquinas's First Three Ways as Christian evidence for God.
lessons.content_html:
Religious Experience as Evidence for God

Religious experience refers to moments when a person feels they have encountered God directly. The Bible records one of the most famous: in Exodus 3, Moses encounters God at the burning bush. A bush burns without being consumed; God calls Moses by name from within it and reveals his divine name and purpose. This experience transforms Moses from a reluctant fugitive into the leader of the Exodus. Christians point to the burning bush as evidence that God communicates directly with human beings and that these encounters have real, life-changing consequences.

Christians across denominations accept religious experience as a genuine route to knowledge of God. Atheists and Humanists challenge this, arguing that religious experiences are subjective inner states that could be produced by the brain, psychological conditioning, or wishful thinking. Richard Dawkins suggests the brain is wired to detect agency and meaning even where none exists. Christians respond that the moral transformation, lasting effects and consistency of religious experiences across vastly different cultures suggest they point to something beyond the individual mind.

Key Fact

Exodus 3 records Moses’s encounter with God at the burning bush — a bush that burned without being consumed. God spoke Moses’s name from the fire and commissioned him to lead the Israelites out of Egypt. Christians use this as evidence that God reveals himself through direct experience, not only through scripture or reason.

Prayer and Answered Prayer

Prayer is central to Christian life, and the experience of answered prayer is used by many Christians as evidence that God is real and responsive. 1 John 5:13–17 teaches that if Christians ask anything “according to his will,” God hears them and grants what they request. This is not a guarantee of receiving whatever is asked but a promise of God’s attentiveness to those who seek him. Christians who report praying for healing, guidance or provision and seeing specific outcomes often cite these experiences as among their strongest reasons for belief.

Atheists and Humanists are sceptical: they argue that apparently answered prayers are explained by coincidence, confirmation bias (noticing the hits and forgetting the misses), or the natural course of events. Studies on the efficacy of intercessory prayer have produced ambiguous results. Christians respond that reducing prayer to an experiment misunderstands its nature — prayer is not a mechanism for testing God but a relationship with a personal God who knows what is best. The claim is not that prayer guarantees specific outcomes but that God is personally present and active in the lives of believers who seek him.

Catholics and many Anglicans emphasise that prayer includes set prayers (the Lord’s Prayer, liturgical forms) that bind the Church across time. Protestant and evangelical Christians often emphasise informal, personal prayer as a direct conversation with God. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians frequently report dramatic answers to prayer including physical healing, which they present as evidence of God’s ongoing miraculous activity. Quakers traditionally practise waiting prayer — silence before God — which is about receptivity rather than petition. All these forms reflect the conviction that God is real and present, but the expectation of specific types of answer varies significantly.

The Design Argument

The design argument proposes that the universe’s order and complexity imply a designer. Paul states in Romans 1:18–24 that God’s “eternal power and divine nature” have been “clearly seen” in creation since the beginning of the world, making those who deny God without excuse. This gives the design argument scriptural support for Christians: the natural world itself testifies to God’s existence.

Paley’s watchmaker analogy from Natural Theology (1802) argues that if you found a watch on a heath, its intricate mechanism would lead you to infer a watchmaker. Living organisms are vastly more complex than any watch. Therefore, they too must have a designer — God. Many Christians find this persuasive: the fine-tuning of physical constants in the universe (the fact that even small changes would make life impossible) seems to point to intentional design.

The Cosmological Argument: Aquinas’s First Three Ways

The cosmological argument argues that the universe’s existence requires a cause beyond itself. Thomas Aquinas presented three forms in his Summa Theologica. His First Way begins from motion: everything moving was moved by something else; there cannot be an infinite chain, so there must be a first unmoved mover — God. His Second Way begins from causation: everything has a cause; there cannot be an infinite chain of causes, so there must be a first uncaused cause — God. His Third Way begins from contingency: things in the universe exist but might not have; there must be a necessary being whose existence is not dependent on anything else — God.

Atheists including Dawkins raise the “who made God?” objection: if everything requires a cause, God must also require a cause. Christians respond (following Aquinas) that God is by definition a necessary being — one who cannot fail to exist and does not require a cause outside himself. The cosmological argument does not say everything has a cause; it says everything that begins to exist or is contingent requires an explanation. Hume challenged whether the premise “every event has a cause” can be established by observation — we only observe causation within the universe, not the universe as a whole. Dawkins also argues that invoking God as the designer simply pushes the problem back: a designer complex enough to create the universe would itself require explanation. Christians respond that Dawkins conflates contingent complexity (which requires explanation) with necessary being (which does not).

Key Fact

Aquinas’s First Three Ways: (1) from motion — everything moved needs a mover, so there is an unmoved mover; (2) from causation — every effect has a cause, so there is a first uncaused cause; (3) from contingency — contingent things might not exist, so there is a necessary being. These are the spec content — the Ontological Argument (Anselm) is not assessed here.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers four arguments in one — make sure you can write specifically about each one rather than blurring them together. The most dangerous error is confusing Aquinas’s Three Ways (a posteriori, from observation) with the Ontological Argument (a priori, from concept alone) — the latter is not on this course. For the 5-mark source question, Romans 1:18–24 is the named biblical anchor for the design argument: cite book, chapter and verse. For prayer as evidence, cite 1 John 5:13–17. For religious experience, Exodus 3 (burning bush). For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Dawkins/Humanist counter-argument fully — one sentence is not enough. SPaG marks: cosmological, contingency, teleological, Aquinas.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religious experience (e.g. Moses at the burning bush, Exodus 3) and answered prayer (1 John 5:13–17) are used by Christians as evidence that God is real and communicates with people; atheists argue these are subjective or coincidental.
  • The design argument (Paley’s watchmaker, Romans 1:18–24) argues natural complexity implies an intelligent creator; Dawkins counters that evolution explains complexity without a designer.
  • Aquinas’s First Three Ways (motion, causation, contingency) are a posteriori cosmological arguments for God as first mover, first cause and necessary being — distinct from the Ontological Argument (not on this course).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious experience is the most convincing evidence that God exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Exodus 3 (Moses), answered prayer (1 John 5:13-17), and the transforming effect of religious experience suggest genuine divine encounter. practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per challenge; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows biological complexity arises through natural selection without requiring a designer — Dawkins calls this a 'blind watchmaker' (2); the existence of suffering and 'bad design' (vestigial organs, disease, extinction) suggests that if the universe was designed, the designer is not all-loving and all-powerful (2); source credit for Romans 1:18-24 used in counter-framing, or Darwin cited explicitly (1).

lessons.title: Religious Upbringing as an Argument
lessons.description: Christian teaching on raising children to believe in God and the indoctrination counter-argument.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Religious Upbringing?

Religious upbringing refers to the process of raising a child within a faith community. For Christians, this typically involves baptism or dedication as an infant, regular prayer at home, church attendance, Sunday school or youth groups, Christian festivals, and where available, faith schools. The sum of these practices creates an environment in which Christian belief feels natural and normal to a child.

Christians cite Proverbs 22:6 as a scriptural foundation: “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.” This verse is understood as both a promise and a command — parents are responsible for giving their children a foundation of faith from the earliest age. The expectation is not that children will be forced to believe but that early formation creates a path they may choose to walk throughout their lives.

Key Fact

Proverbs 22:6: “Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it.” Christians use this verse to support the practice of raising children within the faith — it implies that early formation shapes character and belief for life. It is the key scriptural anchor for this argument.

Features of Christian Upbringing and Why They May Lead to Belief

A Christian upbringing works through several interlocking practices. Prayer at home — saying grace before meals, bedtime prayers — models an ongoing relationship with God as natural and routine. Attending church gives the child a community of believers who reinforce Christian identity and demonstrate that faith is practised by real adults they love and respect. Christian festivals — Christmas, Easter, Pentecost — give rhythm and meaning to the year, connecting the child to the story of Jesus from infancy. Faith schools integrate religious teaching across the curriculum and ensure that Christian values shape the whole learning environment.

For many Christians who now hold strong belief as adults, they trace their faith to this kind of early formation. The experience of worshipping, praying and hearing scripture as a child creates deep neural and emotional pathways that can anchor belief through the challenges of adulthood. Religious upbringing is considered a potential argument for the existence of God — the fact that millions of people retain Christian belief formed in childhood suggests that early formation transmits something real, not merely cultural habit.

The Challenge: Could Upbringing Lead Away from Belief?

Religious upbringing does not guarantee lifelong belief. Many people raised in Christian households later abandon their faith entirely. They may encounter intellectual challenges (the problem of evil, science and religion) that the faith of their childhood cannot answer, or they may experience hurt or hypocrisy within their church community that erodes trust. This is a genuine counter to the argument that upbringing provides evidence for God: if the belief it produces can be undermined by experience and reflection, perhaps it was never based on truth in the first place — just on socialisation.

Indoctrination is the charge that religious upbringing instils beliefs in children before they are old enough to question or evaluate them. Richard Dawkins argues forcefully in The God Delusion (2006) that there is no such thing as a “Christian child” or a “Muslim child” — only children of Christian or Muslim parents. He contends that describing a child by their parents’ religion and subjecting them to religious education before they can think critically is comparable to any other form of intellectual coercion, and amounts to a form of harm. Humanists similarly argue that children have a right to grow up and reach their own conclusions about religion, and that confessional religious education in faith schools violates this right.

Christians respond to the indoctrination charge on several grounds. First, all upbringings involve values — every family raises its children in particular moral and cultural frameworks, including secular ones. Humanists who raise children with naturalistic assumptions are also forming their children’s worldview before the child is old enough to evaluate it. Second, Christian upbringing at its best does not suppress questioning — good Christian education teaches the reasons for faith and invites honest engagement with doubt. Third, the adult who freely chooses to continue in Christian faith, having had the opportunity to walk away, is not a victim of indoctrination but a person who has made an informed decision. The fact that many people raised in Christian homes later leave the faith shows that the process does not simply produce robots who cannot think; conversely, the fact that many stay shows the faith has genuine staying power.

Key Fact

Dawkins argues in The God Delusion (2006) that labelling children with their parents’ religion before they can evaluate it is a form of harm. Christians respond that all upbringings involve values; that good Christian education invites genuine questioning; and that the adult who freely continues in faith has not been indoctrinated but has made an informed choice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This is a short spec point (3B 1.8) but it generates rich discussion questions. For the 5-mark source answer, Proverbs 22:6 is the named anchor — use the book, chapter and verse. For the 12-mark Discuss, present Dawkins’s indoctrination argument fully (not just in one sentence) and give the Christian responses in equal depth. A common error is to treat religious upbringing as a weak argument and spend most of the 12 marks attacking it — remember to argue both sides with equal development. For the 3-mark Outline question, give three discrete features of Christian upbringing (e.g. baptism, Sunday school, prayer at home) as separate bullet-style points, not one extended answer. SPaG: indoctrination, upbringing, Proverbs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Proverbs 22:6 (“start children off on the way they should go”) is the scriptural foundation for Christian religious upbringing — early faith formation is seen as a parental responsibility that shapes lifelong belief.
  • Features of a Christian upbringing include prayer, church attendance, baptism, faith schools and Christian festivals — these create an environment in which belief feels natural and may become personally held.
  • Dawkins argues religious upbringing is a form of indoctrination that harms children by instilling beliefs before they can evaluate them critically; Christians respond that all upbringings instil values and that mature faith is freely chosen.

lessons.title: Marriage, Sexual Relationships and Family
lessons.description: Catholic teaching on marriage as a sacrament, sexual relationships, and the purpose of family in the 21st century.
lessons.content_html:
Marriage as a Sacrament

Marriage occupies a central place in Catholic life. For Catholics, marriage is not simply a social or legal arrangement — it is a sacrament of marriage, one of the seven sacraments through which God’s grace is communicated. The couple are themselves the ministers of the sacrament — they confer it on each other through their freely given, permanent vows, witnessed by the priest and community. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2360–2365 sets out the essential properties of marriage: unity (one husband, one wife), indissolubility (lifelong commitment) and openness to procreation.

Pope Francis addressed the meaning of marriage in his speech “Not Just Good But Beautiful” at the Humanum Conference in November 2014. He described marriage as a “beautiful” vocation that reflects the covenant between Christ and the Church, and lamented that contemporary culture has reduced marriage to a transient arrangement rather than a total gift of self. For Catholics, the permanence of the marriage vow — “what God has joined together, let no one separate” — is a reflection of the faithful, unconditional love of God himself.

Key Fact

Pope Francis’s address “Not Just Good But Beautiful” was given at the Humanum Conference in November 2014. It presents Catholic marriage as beautiful because it reflects Christ’s covenant with the Church — total, permanent and fruitful. It is one of the Edexcel-named sources for Catholic teaching on marriage.

Sexual Relationships: Marital, Unitive and Procreative

Catholic teaching holds that sexual relationships are only appropriate within marriage. The Catechism (CCC 2360–2365) identifies three essential dimensions of marital sexuality. First, sex is marital — confined to the marriage relationship. Second, it is unitive — it deepens and expresses the loving bond between spouses, strengthening the covenant. Third, it is procreative — it must remain open to new life. Catholic teaching insists that the unitive and procreative dimensions cannot be artificially separated. To remove the procreative dimension deliberately (as artificial contraception does) is to violate the full meaning of the sexual act.

On same-sex relationships, the Catechism teaches that while individuals with same-sex attraction deserve respect and compassion, same-sex sexual activity does not correspond to the marital vocation as the Church understands it. This is one of the most debated areas of Catholic ethics in contemporary society, with divergent views within Christianity: many Protestant denominations and the Church of England now affirm same-sex partnerships, reflecting a different interpretation of scripture and tradition. Catholics are called to treat everyone with dignity while maintaining the teaching on marriage.

Many Protestant churches and some Anglican denominations accept sexual relationships outside marriage and same-sex partnerships, arguing that love and commitment are the core Christian values rather than the legal form. Non-religious (Humanist and atheist) views generally hold that consensual sexual relationships between adults are morally acceptable regardless of marital status, and that human wellbeing and equality are the key ethical tests. The Catholic Church responds that its teaching is grounded in natural law (the purpose of sex as written into human nature) and in scripture, not merely in social convention, and that redefining marriage or sexuality ultimately harms human flourishing even if it appears liberating in the short term.

The Purpose and Importance of Family

For Catholics, the family is “the domestic church” — the first place where faith is lived and passed on. The primary purposes of marriage include procreation and the education of children in the faith. Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981), sections 36–85, provides the most detailed modern Catholic teaching on the family. It describes the family as the “first and vital cell of society” and outlines four specific tasks: forming a community of persons, serving life, participating in the development of society, and sharing in the life and mission of the Church.

Catholics do not ignore the reality of diverse family structures in 21st-century society. The Church recognises that families today include nuclear, single-parent, same-sex parent, extended, and blended families. The Catholic response is pastoral rather than condemnatory — families who do not match the ideal are still offered the full support of the Church community, while the Church maintains its teaching about the ideal of marriage between a man and a woman.

Key Fact

Familiaris Consortio was written by Pope John Paul II in 1981. It describes the family as the “first and vital cell of society” and the “domestic church.” It gives four tasks of the family: community of persons, serving life, developing society, and sharing in the Church’s mission. Sections 36–85 cover the family directly.

Support from the Local Parish: Family Group Movement

The local Catholic parish supports families through family worship, sacramental preparation, parents’ classes, children’s groups and counselling. One concrete example the spec names is the Family Group Movement, founded in France in 1947. Small groups of families meet regularly for prayer, discussion and practical support, creating a community in which faith can be shared and family life strengthened. The Catechism 2226 also notes that parents are “the first educators” of their children in the faith — the parish exists to support them in that primary vocation, not to replace it.

Cohabitation (living together as an unmarried couple) is viewed negatively in official Catholic teaching, because the permanence and public commitment of marriage are seen as essential to the full meaning of the sexual relationship. Many non-religious people and some Protestants regard cohabitation as a reasonable way to test compatibility before marriage, and argue that committed relationships have the same moral value whether legally formalised or not. The Catholic Church responds that the absence of a binding commitment changes the nature of the relationship and undermines the conditions for genuine self-gift. It nevertheless recognises that pastoral sensitivity is required when working with cohabiting couples who may be seeking to grow closer to the Church.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This topic has several named papal documents that must appear in 5-mark source answers: “Not Just Good But Beautiful” (Pope Francis, 2014) for marriage; Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981) for family. For Catechism references: CCC 2360–2365 covers sexual relationships (marital, unitive, procreative); CCC 2226 covers parents as first educators. Use the technical terms “unitive” and “procreative” in your answers — they appear in the mark schemes for Catholic paper questions. For the 12-mark Discuss, develop both the Catholic position and the non-religious view equally — do not just list one sentence on each side. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of: sacrament, procreative, Familiaris Consortio.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Marriage is a sacrament in Catholic teaching: permanent, exclusive, and open to life. Pope Francis’s “Not Just Good But Beautiful” (2014) describes it as reflecting Christ’s covenant love.
  • Catholic teaching (CCC 2360–2365) insists sexual relationships must be marital, unitive, and procreative — these three properties cannot be artificially separated.
  • Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981) calls the family the “domestic church” and the “first and vital cell of society,” with support offered through the local parish including the Family Group Movement and Catechism 2226.

lessons.title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination
lessons.description: Catholic teaching on contraception, divorce, the equality of men and women, and gender prejudice.
lessons.content_html:
Family Planning and Contraception

The Catholic Church teaches that artificial contraception is morally wrong. This position is most clearly stated in Humanae Vitae (1968), written by Pope Paul VI. The document argues that every act of sexual intercourse must remain open to both its unitive dimension (deepening love between spouses) and its procreative dimension (openness to new life). Deliberately removing the procreative dimension through artificial means — the contraceptive pill, condoms, sterilisation — violates the integrity of the sexual act as God intended it.

The Church does not oppose natural family planning (NFP), which works with the body’s natural fertility cycles. NFP methods (such as monitoring the woman’s cycle to identify fertile and infertile periods) are not considered contraception in the moral sense because no act of intercourse is deliberately made infertile — instead, couples abstain during fertile periods. Catholics who use NFP still respect the principle that each act of intercourse must remain open to life in principle.

Key Fact

Humanae Vitae was published in 1968 by Pope Paul VI. It forbids the use of artificial contraception on the grounds that the unitive and procreative dimensions of marriage cannot be artificially separated. It remains one of the most debated documents in modern Catholic history.

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept artificial contraception as a responsible way to plan a family. They argue that responsible parenthood and the wellbeing of existing children and the mother are important factors that a fixed rule about every act cannot accommodate. From the perspective of situation ethics (Joseph Fletcher, 1966), each case should be decided by what maximises love (agape) — and for a couple in poverty or with health concerns, contraception may be the most loving choice. Humanists and atheists generally see contraception as a tool of responsible reproductive choice with no moral problem. Catholics respond that the Church’s teaching is not merely a rule but a statement about the nature of sexual love, and that following it requires virtue, not restriction.

Divorce, Annulment and Remarriage

Divorce is not recognised by the Catholic Church as a valid dissolution of a sacramental marriage. Because marriage is a sacrament — a permanent covenant before God — it cannot simply be dissolved by a civil court. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2382–2386 acknowledges that civil divorce may sometimes be justified as a legal measure to protect financial and civil rights, particularly in cases of abuse or abandonment. But in Catholic teaching, the person remains married before God even after a civil divorce. Remarrying while a first spouse is still living is therefore regarded as adultery.

The Church does, however, offer the process of annulment. This is not the same as divorce — it does not dissolve a marriage but declares that a valid sacramental marriage never existed from the beginning, because one or both parties lacked the capacity, freedom or intention required for a valid marriage. If a marriage is annulled, both parties are free to marry in the Church. Annulments require an investigation by a Church tribunal and are not automatic.

Key Fact

Catechism 2382–2386: civil divorce does not dissolve a sacramental marriage before God. Remarriage after divorce without annulment is regarded as adultery. Annulment is the Church’s ruling that a valid sacramental marriage never existed — not a Catholic divorce. Distinction is crucial in the exam.

Equality of Men and Women in the Family

Catholic teaching holds that men and women are equal in dignity before God but have complementary roles in the family. Catechism 2207 states that the family is “the original cell of social life” and that within the family, both parents have essential roles. The Church values what it calls “the dignity of work within the home” — the contribution of whoever carries out domestic and childcare work, whether mother or father, is considered genuinely valuable and not less important than paid employment.

Pope John Paul II’s “theology of the body” (a series of catechetical lectures given 1979–1984) offers a deeper philosophical framework. John Paul II argued that the body itself is a “theology” — its sexual differentiation as male and female reflects the self-giving love that defines the Trinity and that finds its human expression in marriage. This approach respects the embodied difference between men and women while insisting on their equal dignity and worth.

Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

The Catholic Church officially opposes all forms of gender prejudice and discrimination. Catechism 1938 states that “every form of social or cultural discrimination in fundamental personal rights on the grounds of sex, race, color, social conditions, language, or religion must be curbed and eradicated as incompatible with God’s design.” This is a strong and explicit statement. Within Catholic families and communities, both men and women should be treated with equal respect and given equal opportunity to develop their gifts.

The question of the role of women in the Church is a point of divergence within Christianity. The Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women as priests, arguing that Jesus chose only male apostles and that this reflects a permanent theological intention, not a cultural accident. The Church of England and most Protestant denominations do ordain women, arguing that the principle of equality in Christ (“there is neither male nor female” — Galatians 3:28) outweighs the argument from historical practice. Catholics respond that women hold vitally important roles in the Church as religious sisters, catechists, liturgical ministers and leaders of lay movements, even without ordination.

Situation ethics, developed by Joseph Fletcher in 1966, argues that love (agape) should guide every moral decision contextually, without rigid rules. Applied to divorce, this might mean that if a marriage has irretrievably broken down and both parties are suffering, the most loving course is separation and the freedom to remarry. Applied to gender roles, situation ethicists would argue that whatever enables human beings to flourish and love one another is morally correct, regardless of traditional role boundaries. Catholics respond that situation ethics sounds compassionate but can justify almost any action if framed in terms of “love,” and that the natural law framework of Catholic ethics provides more reliable guidance for human flourishing over time than case-by-case judgement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The two most important named sources for this lesson are Humanae Vitae (Pope Paul VI, 1968) on contraception and Catechism 2382–2386 on divorce and annulment. In the exam, state these precisely: “In Humanae Vitae (1968), Pope Paul VI taught that artificial contraception violates the unitive and procreative nature of marriage.” For gender, the source is Catechism 1938 (opposition to discrimination) and Catechism 2207 (family as cell of society). Do not confuse annulment with divorce — annulment declares a marriage was never valid; divorce dissolves a valid marriage. The Catholic Church recognises the former but not the latter. SPaG marks: spell Humanae Vitae, “annulment,” “contraception” correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Humanae Vitae (Pope Paul VI, 1968) forbids artificial contraception: every act of sex must remain open to life. Natural family planning is permitted because it works with fertility rather than against it.
  • Catholic teaching (CCC 2382–2386) does not recognise divorce of a valid sacramental marriage. Annulment declares a marriage was never valid; it is not divorce. Remarriage after divorce without annulment is considered adultery.
  • Men and women are equal in dignity (CCC 1938 opposes all gender discrimination). Pope John Paul II’s theology of the body argues that the body’s sexual complementarity reflects the self-giving love of the Trinity.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Catholic view: Humanae Vitae (1968, Paul VI) argues that separating unitive and procreative dimensions violates the nature of marriage; natural law supports this. Counter: most Protestant churches accept contraception as responsible family planning; situation ethics (Fletcher, 1966) would say the loving choice should guide each case; Humanists argue reproductive autonomy is a basic right. Evaluate which case is stronger. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: Humanae Vitae, contraception, procreative.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which divergent Christian views about divorce and remarriage differ from Catholic teaching, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Many Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage, arguing that the compassionate response to an irretrievably broken marriage is freedom to begin again rather than lifelong legal commitment to a dead relationship (2); the Catholic Church, by contrast, teaches that CCC 2382-2386 does not permit remarriage after divorce of a valid sacramental marriage, as marriage is a permanent covenant before God (2); source credit for CCC 2382-2386 or Humanae Vitae cited explicitly (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What did Humanae Vitae (1968) by Pope Paul VI teach about contraception?
options: Natural family planning is forbidden but artificial methods are permitted
Artificial contraception is forbidden because every act of sex must remain open to life

knowledge_checks.q: What is a Catholic annulment?
options: A Catholic form of divorce that ends a valid marriage
A declaration that a valid marriage never existed from the beginning
Permission to remarry after the death of a spouse
A Church ceremony recognising a civil divorce

Civil divorce does not dissolve a sacramental marriage
Gender discrimination is incompatible with God's design

glossary_terms.definition: A 1968 encyclical by Pope Paul VI reaffirming Catholic opposition to artificial contraception, arguing the unitive and procreative dimensions of sex cannot be separated.
Methods of spacing pregnancies that work with the body's natural fertility cycles rather than using artificial barriers or chemicals — accepted by the Catholic Church.
The legal dissolution of a marriage — the Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved.
A Church tribunal ruling that a marriage was never valid in the first place — not a Catholic divorce, but a declaration that no true sacramental marriage existed.
Pope John Paul II's series of catechetical lectures (1979-1984) presenting Catholic teaching on human sexuality and marriage as a total gift of self.
An ethical theory developed by Joseph Fletcher (1966) arguing that the loving action in each unique situation should guide moral decisions rather than fixed rules.
Unfair treatment of a person on the grounds of their gender — opposed by the Catholic Church in Catechism 1938.
